source_refs.note: Topic 23.6 with Table 23.1 and Quick Check 23.4, answered (PDF 111-112); the structures are redrawn. The book labels the H of methanoic acid '(-I effect)'; the lesson explains the difference by the +I effect of the methyl group. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than phenols, and phenols are more acidic than alcohols. The strength of an acid, the extent to which it ionises, depends on the stability of its conjugate base. For ethanoic acid, CH3COOH <=> CH3COO- + H+, Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5 and pKa = 4.76.

blocks.alt: Ethanoic acid, CH3-C(=O)-O-H, with -delta on the O and +delta on the H, in equilibrium (H2O over the arrows) with the ethanoate ion, CH3-C(=O)-O-, + H+. Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5; pKa = 4.76.
blocks.caption: Ionisation of ethanoic acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.title: pKa
blocks.text: pKa = -log Ka. The higher the Ka, or the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid.

In the ethanoate ion the negative charge is not held on one oxygen: the electrons are delocalised over the -COO- group, so the charge is shared by both oxygens. This stabilises the ethanoate ion and makes it less likely to accept an H+ ion and re-form the undissociated acid.

blocks.alt: Two resonance structures of the ethanoate ion joined by a double-headed arrow: CH3-C(=O)-O- and CH3-C(-O-)=O. Curly arrows show the C=O pi electrons moving onto one oxygen and a lone pair of the O- moving back into the C-O bond.
blocks.caption: Delocalisation of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.text: Substituents change the acidity. An electron-donating group (+I effect) destabilises the carboxylate ion by intensifying its negative charge, and so weakens the acid. An electron-withdrawing group (-I effect) stabilises the carboxylate ion by spreading its negative charge, and so strengthens the acid. Methanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 x 10^-4, pKa 3.75) is ten times stronger than ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5, pKa 4.75), because the methyl group of ethanoic acid is electron-donating. Chlorine atoms are strongly electron-withdrawing, so each extra chlorine makes the acid stronger.

blocks.alt: H-COOH with the H boxed in yellow and an arrow down to '(-I effect)'; Ka = 1.8 x 10^-4, pKa = 3.75. CH3-COOH with the CH3 boxed and an arrow down to '(+I effect)'; Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5, pKa = 4.75.
blocks.caption: Methanoic acid and ethanoic acid compared (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.alt: Displayed formulas of acetic acid (pKa = 4.74), chloroacetic acid (2.86), dichloroacetic acid (1.26) and trichloroacetic acid (0.64): one, two and three H atoms on the CH3 carbon are replaced by Cl. A pink block arrow pointing right is labelled 'Stronger acid'.
blocks.caption: Acetic acid and its chloro-substituted acids (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).
